paper_title: EmoReward: Self-Evolving Reward Calibration for Emotional Video Generation RL

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) has advanced generative model post-training in verifiable domains such as code and mathematics, but evaluating video quality, especially emotional expression, often depends on subjective aesthetics and has no uniquely correct target. Existing approaches typically rely on fixed rewards for visual quality, motion quality, and text alignment that poorly capture emotional intent and can invite reward hacking, while RLHF is difficult to scale and subject to individual aesthetic differences that complicate the calibration of facial, body motion, and chromatic cues across narrative contexts. We introduce EmoReward, a new self-evolving training mechanism that distills evidence reliability from reward traces collected during an actual training run to adaptively guide multi-reward weight allocation in subsequent training by determining which emotional evidence to trust and how much to weight it. EmoReward first plans specific grounding cues from the emotional prompt to guide evaluation, then uses heterogeneous signal primitives to score the generated video during the act stage. Reflective Reward Gating calibrates their contributions through instance-level gates for phase, face confidence, conflict, and subtlety, then renormalizes weights over the active set to produce the sample's fused reward. RewardMemory then estimates each primitive's reliability from rollout scores and outcomes within each emotional regime in the finished training run, then fixes bounded multipliers that calibrate fusion weights in the next training run without updating reward models. Experiments on HunyuanVideo 1.5 show improvements across multiple RL algorithms and compare EmoReward with other agentic reward methods under SAGE-GRPO. Ablations and transfer experiments on SD 3.5 and FLUX further support adaptive reward calibration for visual generation.

sections.title:
1 Introduction
Reinforcement learning (RL), especially Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), has advanced model
post-training in verifiable domains such as code and mathematics, where correctness provides a direct learning
signal [16, 46, 50, 75]. In contrast, evaluating video quality, especially emotional expression, often depends
on subjective aesthetics and has no uniquely correct target. Visual post-training adapts diffusion and flow
generators through RL and preference objectives [2, 12, 29, 43, 60, 72, 82]. Learned evaluators provide scores
for image preference and video quality [17, 22, 30, 38, 68, 69], but a visually clear, temporally stable video can
match its prompt without conveying the intended emotion. Facial analysis, dynamic expression recognition,
and multimodal emotion models supply complementary evidence [1, 3, 7, 26, 79], whose reliability varies with
context: facial cues require visible faces, strong motion can undermine restrained sadness, and saturated
colors may reflect style rather than emotional intent. This raises a central question: Which emotional evidence
should the reward system trust in the current video, and how can it adaptively determine how much weight to
assign to that evidence?
Agentic systems coordinate interaction, refine outputs through feedback, and organize evaluation into rubrics
[15, 39, 47, 62, 65]. These capabilities motivate adaptive evaluation, yet existing video GRPO methods
typically rely on fixed rewards for visual quality, motion quality, and text alignment that inadequately capture
emotional intent. Reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) and preference optimization address
subjective goals [8, 41, 44, 48], but human annotation is costly at scale, and aesthetic differences complicate
the calibration of emotional cues across contexts. Fixed fusion can mix informative, missing, and saturated
signals, allowing policy updates to exploit scoring shortcuts rather than improve emotional fidelity. This
motivates reward calibration at two complementary levels: assessing which cues are valid within each video,
and learning from a completed training run how much those cues should influence rewards in the next run.
sections.content: We introduce EmoReward, self-evolving training mechanism for emotional video-generation RL (Figure 1). It distills evidence reliability from rewardoutcome traces collected during an actual, completed training run, then uses this experience to guide multi-reward weight allocation in the next run to decide which emotional evidence to trust and how much to weight it. Plan translates emotional intent into an EmoScript specifying 2 affect targets, facial and body cues, and an expression window; Act scores generated videos with heterogeneous primitives, keeping criterion scores separate from evidence validity. Within each video, Reflective Reward Gating calibrates these cues using the training phase, face confidence, semantic conflict, and subtlety, then renormalizes weights over active providers. After training run, RewardMemory estimates provider reliability for each emotional regime from traces. Providers with stronger agreement are given larger weight multipliers for the next run, with limits on the size of the adjustment. These multipliers and all reward models stay fixed throughout that run; for each new video, reflection further downweights or excludes missing or unsuitable cues before the active scores are combined into weighted average EmoReward can be integrated into several RL algorithms alongside general video rewards, and directly use training experience to calibrate reward allocation without retraining the evaluators. We evaluate EmoReward on HunyuanVideo 1.5 [64] with DanceGRPO [72], FlowGRPO [29], and SAGEGRPO [82], observing higher VideoAlign scores for the guided configurations across all three RL algorithms on emotional prompts as the evaluation dataset for rollout. Under fair comparison on the same RL architecture and training budget, EmoReward achieves the highest reliability selectivity and both composite calibration scores among seven reward policies. Ablation studies and mechanism analyses examine the contributions of reflective gating, provider pools, and RewardMemory (Section 4.2). Transfer experiments on Stable Diffusion 3.5 and FLUX show gains in selected configurations alongside objective-dependent trade-offs, while user studies show that EmoReward receives the highest human preference and proportion of Good ratings and the lowest proportion of Bad ratings for emotional fidelity, temporal coherence, and visual quality. Our contributions are threefold. We introduce EmoReward, to our knowledge the first self-evolving training mechanism for emotional video generation RL that calibrates reward providers across training runs without updating reward model parameters. We propose RewardMemory, to our knowledge the first memory designed for multi-reward systems in video generation. It distills evidence reliability into bounded fusion weights, enabling iterative calibration of RL reward signals across training runs. We inspire novel cross-run self-evolution paradigm for post-training multimodal foundation models: completed training run informs reward allocation in the next, making training experience reusable at the run level. Extensive experiments across three video RL algorithms and two image backbones, with ablations and human evaluations, validate EmoRewards effectiveness.

sections.title:
2 Related Work
From verifiable RL to agentic feedback for non-verifiable rewards. RLHF learns subjective preferences
[8, 41], whereas verifiable RL exploits correctness checks [16, 75]. Agentic evaluators [9, 77] and adaptive
rubrics [15, 70, 78] structure open-ended feedback. Related approaches route experts [40], refine responses
[39], evolve rewards [35, 76], or organize experience [47, 71]. JitRL derives closed-form policy updates from
retrieved action advantages [25]. EmoReward instead transfers reward–outcome evidence across completed
training runs to calibrate frozen providers, combining sample-level gating with persistent fusion weights.
sections.content: Agents for visual content creation. Agentic visual creation organizes generation into planning, tool use, and feedback-driven refinement. Video agents coordinate multi-shot narratives, script evaluation, audiovisual planning, and learned camera control[11, 18, 59, 67, 80, 81]. Image agents combine knowledge retrieval [4, 14], learned creation and editing policies [23, 27], and experience reuse [5, 6]. Other approaches jointly improve generation and evaluation [28, 51]. EmoReward naturally achieves self-evolving mechanism in video generation RL training, rather than building workflow or retraining reward models. RLHF for visual generation and the emotion-reward gap. Visual reward models capture preferences and multidimensional quality [22, 30, 38, 63, 66, 68, 69]. Optimization using rewards and preferences extends from images [2, 12, 43, 60] to video and flow models [29, 31, 72, 82], with benchmarks assessing quality and compositional alignment [20, 32, 49]. Related 3D, audiovisual, and objectives for human animation address complementary aspects of visual generation [19, 24, 55, 56]. Distillation [13, 21, 74] and feature reuse [34] improve generation efficiency, complementing reward-based post-training. Affect-grounded augmentation [61] and reflective actionconditioned generation [73] further connect feedback with video synthesis. Temporal video modeling and dynamic facial-expression recognition provide additional perceptual foundations [3, 52]. Emotion understanding supplies multimodal evidence [7, 26, 79] and grounded affect representations [1, 10, 45]; EmoReward addresses how their reliability should govern reward fusion across scenes and training runs.

4.4 Human evaluation
Eighteen participants rated the three methods on 30 prompts using Bad/Normal/Good for emotion fidelity,
temporal coherence, and visual quality. Table 3 shows that EmoReward obtains the highest Good shares
(60.0%, 54.3%, 57.2%), compared with 53.0%, 51.5%, and 45.0% for SAGE-GRPO, and the lowest Bad shares
on all three criteria. These descriptive results complement the automatic metrics; aggregation and statistical
scope are detailed in Appendix B.
sections.content: The complete distributions reveal distinction that Good shares alone obscure: SAGE-GRPO also receives more Bad ratings than GT on every criterion. EmoReward lowers Bad shares relative to both comparison groups while increasing Good shares. This pattern supports examining the entire ordinal distribution, rather than reducing it to binary preference. The reported margins do not resolve variation across people or prompts; participantand prompt-level records are required for uncertainty estimates that account for repeated judgments.

sections.title:
5 Conclusion
In this paper, we proposed EmoReward, a self-evolving reward calibration framework for emotional video
generation reinforcement learning. EmoReward combines instance-level Reflective Reward Gating with
RewardMemory, which transfers provider-reliability estimates from a completed training run to subsequent
optimization without updating reward-model parameters. Experiments across video optimizers, complemented
by ablations, image-transfer analyses, and human ratings, support the utility of adaptive calibration while
identifying objective-dependent trade-offs. These findings suggest that completed-run experience can inform
the allocation of trust among heterogeneous reward providers, providing a foundation for further research on
reward-system evolution across training.
